Messages.Author: Jay Kristoff
Messages.Body:
Wes wrote:
>I can't seem to find the VEKN tournament rule forcing players
>to "maximize VPs". Could someone please tell me where to
>find this information?

There is no such rule. Darwin never said "survival of the fittest",
and neither the V:TES nor V:EKN rules say "maximize your victory
points". The closest thing to this comes from the standard rules
under the object of the game: "Your goal is to accumulate the most
victory points by destroying the influence held by rival Methuselahs."
It was recently explained to me that "most", in that object clause,
means "more than anyone else" and not "as many as possible".
I believe that it is from that clause that the confusion comes.
Having to maximize one's VPs would cause all sorts of troubles
when it came to deal making and keeping.

word up,
Jay

Messages.Author: Timlagor
Messages.Body:


Incorrect.
{I've always wanted to do that ;-D}

There is such a rule. If it isn't in the tournament rules it should be. LSJ
made a ruling but I can't find it -search on "author: LSJ" and any othe
suitable term in Google for this group and you will get some references to
it but I didn't find the actual ruling. (I'm sure someone else will point it
out shortly ;-)

Anyway:

1) You must try to get a Table/Game Win
2) If you cannot achieve a Win, you must maximise your Victory Points.
3) You may choose to honour a deal that contravenes (1) or (2) above IF and
ONLY IF that deal was in line with the rules (including 1 and 2 above) at
the time you made it.
(ie. if you make a deal that improves your situation, you are allowed to
complete it even if it would be in your interests to break it -having
already benefitted earlier but not yet completed your part of the bargain).

EG: You make a deal with your predator that he will help you kill your prey
(who you have no prospect of ousting without active help from your predator)
and then let him oust you. Assuming that you genuinely couldn't have ousted
your prey without this help, it is legal to let your predator oust you
afterwards even if you could then prevent them from doing so.
If on the other hand you make a deal to throw the game at a point where you
have a decent prospect of winning you MUST break that deal if breaking it
will gain you VP/a win.

It is legal to make a deal that reduces your chance of winning/VPs so long
as you don't intend to honour it. It is not legal to honour such a deal
later (when it comes to the point where it costs you VP)

It is *ALWAYS LEGAL* to break a (cardless) deal.
(Succubus Club is the obvious exception where the deal resolves all at once
anyway -afaik- you can make a deal to exchange stuff with SC and then do
something else such as not attack and break the later part of the deal: just
not the exchange). I'm sure LSJ will let us know if this is right :-)

LSJ: Is there any reason I can't attach a penalty clause to my deal?
Something along the lines of "I'll do X and in exchange you'll do Y. If you
fail to do Y I will throw all my resources into ousting you without any
further regard to my prospects of winning or gaining VP." Or rather could
such a deal be legal to honour in the breach <;-)>? I reckon it could on the
grounds that it increases the chances of the deal being honoured and thus
(assuming a beneficial deal which would be required anyway) your chance of
VPs (though maybe not always).

Messages.Author: LSJ
Messages.Body:
Timlagor wrote:
> Sure. I realise that -but is it *legal to honour* such a deal in the even
> that your 'partner' fails to do his part and you get to invoke the penalty
> clause?

"Is it legal to honor a broken deal?"
is a flawed question.

The threat of action if the other person breaks the deal is just that, a
threat. It is not a deal. Adding the clause doesn't improve your chances
of winning or of increasing VPs. But, as long as "honoring" the penalty
clause doesn't hurt your chances, then, like any other activity that
doesn't hurt your chances, you're free to do so.

Messages.Author: DeistMutts
Messages.Body:
Ok.. let's get cynical about this topic. So tell me the following if
legal or not:

1) A, B, C remaining at the tournament table as the predator/prey
order: A and B both got 1 VP. C made deal with A to oust B so that A
can get 2 VP, and C will have a chance to tie the table with 2VP
knowing he could've just try to oust A and get B afterwards to win the
table. Is C's motive legal?

2) A, B, C remaining at the tournament table as the predator/prey
order: A already ousted 2, and got 2VPs, B and C didn't get any yet. C
never pressured A in whole game and A ended up 4-5 minions while C had
only one big vampire with 1 blood but really nice pool recursion. A is
'worried' C might get chance to oust him, and made deal with B that
they would both oust C out first and then deal with each other. Is A
motive legal?

3) A, B, C remaining at the tournament table as the predator/prey
order: A already ousted 2, and got 2 VPs, and thinks his deck will
cremate B's deck theme, so he decided to go fully backwards and take C
out and give B the 1VP. However, B ended up easily defeating A
afterwards and got 3vp instead. Is A motive legal?

My above points are simply as this, we all can try to win the game by
how we think, but if one doesn't like the other, he can just try to
find some 'reasonable' excuse to oust that other player and get away
with it. Ruling has nothing to do with it since it is nearly
impossible to pose a judgement on such activity. It's like hiring
minorities in coaching NFL(oh no, the racial issue.. but sorry, this
is the most obvious example that I think many can understand) but you
want certain type of ppl (friends, etc), and so you say 'well, I dont
want this candidate around because i think the team has a better
chance to win with this other candidate's philosophy'.. better yet,
the game show "Weakest Link", where many of the smartest/wittiest ppl
were ousted by peers' votes because they pose threat, or simply,
unlikeable..

Therefore my observation is such... You CAN'T impose ruling on ousting
in some situations where it's just a big fat grey area using the
excuse "I must TRY to get a table/game win".. even great judges cannot
judge by themselves what is right and wrong sometimes. You can try to
find proof that A and B are great friends and planned to take out
anyone else in tournament, but without solid proof of such plans, and
along with very smart careful moves, you can avoid to be caught
'cheating'. So is life. It is ridiculous to make such ruling if no
solid proof is found or if everyone is cunning enough to avoid getting
caught. The only thing you can do is.. always remember who did that to
you, and make sure they learn their lessions not to mess with you next
time, or ever, in next game. Glad V:tES is just a game? :)

lucky break.

If there was a problem with A's behaviour, however, then the judge would
have to make a judgement call on whether *he* thought A was playing to
win. You can't judge people's motives per se, just what the possible or
probably effects will be on their TWs or VPs.

Messages.Author: Ira
Messages.Body:
Hey LSJ and Whoever has control over the tournament rules,

I think the common definition of "sportsmanship" is sufficiently
different from the way we define it for V:TES tournaments that it
should be clarified in the tournament rules. This has come up over
and over, and the following text (which reflects the reality of the
tournament rules) should be explicitly added to the tournament rules:

****************************
- You must try to get a Game Win
- If you don't have a reasonable chance of getting a Game Win, you
must try to maximize your VPs.
- If you don't have a reasonable chance of getting more than zero VPs,
you can play however you want (oust yourself, kingmaker, wall, etc.)
- You may choose to honor a deal that goes against the above rules if
the deal was legally made.

"A reasonable chance" is decided by the judge.
****************************

From talking with LSJ, "a reasonable chance" should be something like
5% to 10%, not 50% or 1%. That's my interpretation of the case
studies provided to LSJ, since he refused to provide even a ballpark
number. :)

I admit that stating actual percentage chances in reality is
impossible, but stating a number as a ballpark figure is helpful to
judges since the definition of "reasonable" could vary so much from
judge to judge, and I don't think we want rulings that vary greatly
from judge to judge.

Ira

Messages.Author: James Coupe
Messages.Body:
In message <bd7l9...@enews4.newsguy.com>, Wes

<gh...@NYETSPAMmnsi.net> writes:
>How can someone self-oust and still be in accordance with the "play to win"
>rule?

If, by so doing, you maximise your Table Wins and VP chances, in the
opinion of the judge, to a reasonable level of confidence.

If you already have a table win, you have 'won' and can win in the
manner you please. (The theoretical problem of players then randomly
giving away VPs is mostly, but not entirely, theoretical. Such
behaviour is likely to reflect on players long term, and a judge paying
attention will likely watch them in later rounds for signs of collusion
etc.)

If you do not have a table win, you must be unable to get a table win
(in the reasonable opinion of the judge). Additionally, you must be
unable (in the...) to get any more VPs than you currently have.

The text book example would be a player who has been pounded into the
ground, who ousts himself because he has no chance of going anywhere.

Additionally, if you had made a legitimate deal earlier, you could oust
yourself in the process of honouring that deal. Remember, the "play to
win" rule doesn't mean that you automatically have to backstab a
legitimate deal. (Due to the inherent problems this would cause with
certain obvious relatively long-term deals, where you could never make
them, since you would automatically be required to backstab the other
player, who would therefore never go through with the deal in the first
place.)

It is possible, for instance, that a player saved you from otherwise
certain death, allowing you to get an otherwise impossible VP, for which
you offered to oust yourself later. e.g. Me, you and LSJ are playing,
that order (add in a couple of other players). LSJ is playing some
nasty intercept, which will be a nightmare to my votes. You're doing
pretty badly and I could otherwise oust you, but I reckon your combat
will help me. So I make a deal with you that I'll help you get LSJ.
Perhaps I call one of my votes - an Archon, which I put in the deck for
bargaining power, perhaps? And this way, you get a VP ousting LSJ, and
you roll over, giving me a VP and a better shot at killing the other two
players because I don't have an intercept wall stopping EVERY SINGLE
VOTE, so I do better. That sort of thing is entirely plausible. You
get a VP you wouldn't/couldn't have got, and in return you stop me
having to fight through you *again*.

Messages.Author: Timlagor
Messages.Body:
> But by paying his last 2 pool, player A is ousting himself and therefore
> *cannot* maximize his chances to win.
>
> How can someone self-oust and still be in accordance with the "play to win"
> rule?

This isn't the situation we were discussing but here is one way:

A B and C left.
A has 2 pts
B has 0 pt
C has 0 pts

B is set to mop up.
A can't (reasonably expect to) oust B.
A believes 6 pool will not allow C to beat B (and probably A believes that B
is likely to oust C next turn -no point doing it prematurely)

A self-ousts.
B ousts C

A 2
B 2
C 1
D/E 0

As you say also the trivial situation where A has already won. In a 6 player
game, A could get an outright win like this.

Messages.Author: Timlagor
Messages.Body:
>>Surely the answer is "NO"? A has no VP and may (however improbably) get one
>>(or half) if he hangs around but can't if he ousts himself. Player B is
>>already showing an inclination to protect A indicating at least some chance
>>he will be around for a timeout.
>
> I don't agree. Player B is clearly attempting to turn "A" into a meat
> shield, allowing B to focus all his efforts on ousting C without any
> pressure from behind.

A becomes a meat shield. B wants to keep him as long as possible and if the
table is going to time out, would rather have him in than out at that point.
Therefore he can be expected to make further moves to keep A in the game.

> The amount of time it would take to oust A, given that he had no
> vampires and ten pool, is equivalent to the speed in which one can say:
>
> "No master. Bleed for 1, bleed for 1, bleed for 1, bleed for 1, no
> discard, done."

1) Assuming A can't get another Vamp out and do soemthing useful with it)
2) Depends how long B's turns are too.

> ...as many times as necessary, and as many vampires as you have who can
> bleed. A has no reasonable chance to survive to a timeout unless there
> is already almost no time left in the round -- either his predator will
> get him, or B will blow through his predator and finish A off himself.

Very probably but you can't be certain. C might decide to hit B hard because
he feels threatened and misjudge it (assuming B can do more to help A).

> I would personally like to see self-ousting made illegal. Transfer

Can't argue with that -well I could but I happen to agree ;-)
OTOH I think that it already is illegal in most circumstances (ie when you
don't want to spread the VPs around to make the ones you have go further)

OK, I'll give you a hint. Chess players think on their opponent's time.

It's very easy to adapt a similar style to V:TES.

In addition, chess players typically adopt an accumulative thinking
pattern -- assess a situation completely at the beginning, then modify
the situation in small increments as necessary depending on what moves
are made. This applies to V:TES, as well. If I see Beast and Theo as
my grandprey, I can easily class the deck as "rush deck", and from there
determine exactly what type over the course of several turns as I
accumulate more data. However, the simple fact that it's a rush deck
lets me know what sort of moves I can expect from it.

This is why you will see long pauses for thought, and then a number of
moves played at lightning speed -- it was all prepared ahead of time.
